expectations.text: The document states what all three proposed options have in common (building an in-house service, the language, the cloud) and treats each shared element as a prior decision with a row or adds an option outside it
expectations.evidence: The commonality is stated — 'Note first what the three offered options actually are: a subset of a **2 × 2** (Lambda | Fargate) × (Aurora | DynamoDB)', plus a 'Constraints already settled' section naming 'Language: Go. All three candidate options in the request were "in Go"' and 'Cloud: AWS. Implied by every option offered'. But two of the three named shared elements are neither treated as a prior decision with a row nor given an option outside them. Go is classified as an externally settled constraint and is explicitly refused a row: 'Go is absent from this table on purpose — it is a settled constraint, not an alternative (see *Constraints already settled*)', and no alternative language appears anywhere; the only follow-up is open question 6, 'Is Go genuinely settled?', which is a question, not a row or an option. AWS gets a single one-line bullet ('Cloud: AWS. Implied by every option offered (Lambda, Fargate, Aurora, DynamoDB)') with no reversal cost and no alternative — C4 (EKS/Kubernetes) is still AWS. Only the build-in-house element is handled as the assertion asks, via S3 ('Keep the vendor / renegotiate (the honest baseline)') and S2 in the Dimension-3 table.

expectations.text: At least one option outside 'build our own service' is analysed in the tradeoff table (for example keep the providers behind a proxy and cache, license the official dataset, renegotiate the contract), plus a do-nothing baseline
expectations.evidence: The 'Dimension 3 — Data sourcing' tradeoff table carries two non-build options with the full pros / cons / risk / impact / probability / mitigation / contingency treatment: 'S2 — Licensed commercial dataset (bulk licence)' ('license the official dataset' in the assertion's own example list) and 'S3 — Keep the vendor / renegotiate (the honest baseline)', whose pros are 'Zero engineering cost; zero legal exposure; no dataset maintenance forever' — a do-nothing baseline. Both feed named outcomes: 'If a licence costs near $4,000/month, do not build — fall back to S3' and, in the flip table, 'The vendor offers a large discount in Phase 0 → S3. Do not build. This RFC becomes the record of why.'

expectations.text: The legal question is marked as blocking with an owner and a date (or explicitly escalated), and the recommendation is stated as conditional on it or the status is kept at proposed
expectations.evidence: The second half passes: the recommendation is explicitly conditional — 'gated on written legal clearance of the dataset (N6) before any build work starts' — and Phase 0 is 'blocking ... Nothing proceeds without this.' The first half fails on both owner and date, by the document's own admission: open question 3 reads '**(N6) Who owns the legal question, and when will the written opinion land?** Which dataset, publisher, and licence version specifically?' — i.e. neither is set. 'Legal's call' names a function, not an owner, and the only time figure is a duration estimate, not a date ('Legal clearance (N6) ... 1w (elapsed, not effort)'; 'Phase 0 — Close the gates (≈ 1 week, blocking)'). Nor is it explicitly escalated: the unresolved blocker is handed back to the requester as a question, with no named party or forum to resolve it and no deadline attached.

expectations.text: The p95 under 100 ms target carries a derivation (a current measured value, an external reference, or a stakeholder commitment) or is explicitly labelled assumed
expectations.evidence: The 100 ms number itself is carried straight through from the request as a given — 'with a target of **p95 under 100 ms**' in Context, and N1 states 'p95 ≤ 100 ms and **p99 ≤ 250 ms**, server-side at the service boundary, measured under 2× observed peak' with no derivation column and no 'assumed' label. What is labelled assumed is only the *condition*, not the target: 'A5 | p95 ≤ 100 ms is **server-side, measured at the service boundary**, not client-observed end-to-end. Basis: Standard reading of a latency target stated for a service.' The document contains no current measured p95 for the incumbent, no external latency reference, and no stakeholder commitment behind the number; open question 4 likewise asks only whether it is server-side or client-observed. The companion p99 ≤ 250 ms is justified in reasoning ('A p95-only target is gameable') but is also underived and unlabelled. By contrast N3's cost target is derived ('an order of magnitude below the US$ 4,000 it replaces'), so the omission is specific to the latency target.

expectations.text: The $4k/month figure is labelled by how it is known and the document names what would confirm it (for example the billing report by SKU)
expectations.evidence: The confirmation half is present — 'Related documents' names 'Current vendor invoice and contract (term, notice period, per-request rate, any minimum commitment)' and 'Vendor request volume and endpoint breakdown for the last 90 days (from the API gateway / vendor dashboard)', with Phase 0 assigned to fetch them. The labelling half fails: the figure is asserted as current fact with no provenance — 'That bill is now around **US$ 4,000/month**, and it is pure variable cost that grows with traffic' — and is used unlabelled thereafter ('the US$ 4,000 it replaces', '~$48k/year saving'). The only hedge concerns the figure's composition inside a different assumption ('A3 ... **Unverified — the US$ 4,000 could equally be a flat enterprise licence**'), which also contradicts Context's unhedged 'it is pure variable cost'. Nowhere is the number marked as requester-stated or unverified where it is introduced or used.

expectations.text: The title and the opening paragraph name the problem to solve, not the product or stack to build
expectations.evidence: The title names the product to build: 'RFC — In-house address lookup and geocoding service'. The opening paragraph does name the problem ('Today, address lookup and geocoding are bought ... the application calls a third-party HTTP API and pays per request. That bill is now around US$ 4,000/month, and it is pure variable cost that grows with traffic'), and a problem statement follows later ('**The problem to solve:** decide the architecture of an in-house address and geocoding service ...' — itself framed around the service). The assertion requires both the title and the opening; the title fails.

expectations.text: Still reaches an explicit recommendation with its decider, consequences and confirmation
expectations.evidence: Recommendation: '**Recommendation: Fargate + Aurora Serverless v2 (PostgreSQL with PostGIS and pg_trgm), in Go — one of the three options offered — gated on written legal clearance of the dataset (N6)**'. Decider: '**Decision style: autocratic.** The technical recommendation is mine to make and I own it', with two parts explicitly delegated (N6 to legal, N4's threshold to the product owner). Consequences are stated, though not under that heading: 'The genuine cost of building is engineering time, not infrastructure — roughly 6–8 engineer-weeks ... plus the N3 maintenance ceiling of ≤ 4 days/quarter, forever ... a permanent tax the vendor currently absorbs', plus the retained vendor fallback (N7) and the owned dataset-refresh pipeline. Confirmation: 'Phase 1 — Latency spike (2–3 days, go/no-go on N1) ... **Gate: if p95 misses 100 ms, switch to D3 before building anything else**', 'Gate: N4 quality parity on the golden set before any real traffic', staged canary observation windows, and N5 dashboards including match rate and dataset version.

claims.claim: Estimated monthly infrastructure for the recommended stack is ≈ $160–195, so cost does not discriminate between the three options
claims.evidence: Line items check out against us-east-1 list rates: Fargate compute 2 × 0.5 vCPU × 730 h × 0.04 = 29.2 (≈ $30); memory 2 × 1 GB × 730 h × 0.0044 = 6.4 (≈ $7); Aurora 2 × 0.5 ACU × 730 h × 0.12 = 87.6 (≈ $88); plus $5–20 storage/IO, $20 ALB, $10–30 telemetry sums to $160–195. The document flags the estimates as unverified and recalls-from-memory, and the conclusion survives the stated error margin.

claims.claim: US$ 4,000/month at commodity geocoding list rates of $4–5 per 1,000 requests implies ≈ 0.8–1M requests/month ≈ 0.3–0.4 req/s average
claims.evidence: 4000 ÷ 5 = 800k and 4000 ÷ 4 = 1M requests; 1M ÷ 2.63M seconds per month ≈ 0.38 req/s. The arithmetic holds and the document labels the input rate as assumed.

claims.claim: The US$ 4,000/month is pure variable cost that grows with traffic
claims.evidence: Contradicted by the document's own A3: 'Unverified — the US$ 4,000 could equally be a flat enterprise licence, in which case volume is unconstrained by this arithmetic.' Context states it as fact without a label; nothing in the inputs establishes it.

claims.claim: DynamoDB cannot satisfy F2 (fuzzy free-text matching) or F4 (nearest-neighbour) as a query engine, and the standard fix (DynamoDB + OpenSearch) costs more than the entire Aurora option
claims.evidence: Technically accurate: DynamoDB has no native full-text/fuzzy matching and no spatial index; KNN requires hand-rolled geohash sort keys with multi-cell fan-out. A managed OpenSearch cluster does exceed the ≈ $160–195 total estimated for the Aurora option.

claims.claim: Lambda cold starts land inside the p95 rather than the p99 because low average volume keeps no pool warm while autocomplete fires bursts of concurrent requests
claims.evidence: A sound argument given the document's own assumption A3 (low, bursty volume) and F2 (per-keystroke autocomplete): concurrent invocations each need their own execution environment. It rests on the unverified A3, which the document states.

claims.claim: Aurora Serverless v2 scale-to-zero has a resume latency measured in seconds, incompatible with a 100 ms p95, so the cluster must sit at minimum capacity 24/7
claims.evidence: Consistent with documented Aurora Serverless v2 auto-pause/resume behaviour. No source is cited for it in this document, but the claim is correct.

uncertainties: All cost figures are 'order-of-magnitude estimates from AWS us-east-1 list prices as I recall them' and explicitly NOT verified
A1 (which of the four capabilities are in scope) is flagged as decisive and would reverse the recommendation if wrong
A3 (request volume, inferred from the bill) is unverified and would break if the $4k is a flat licence
A4 (dataset fits in container memory) unverified; the 6–8 engineer-week estimate is 'a guess'
needs_review: Owner and landing date of the blocking legal opinion are unknown (open question 3)
Whether 100 ms is server-side or client-observed (open question 4); if client-observed, none of the three options suffices
N4 quality-parity threshold is left to the product owner
workarounds: Go excluded from the tradeoff table as a settled constraint, with a note asking whether it is in fact still open
Recommendation gated on Phase 0 rather than approved, and D3 (in-process index) kept as the documented escape hatch
